label: Claude Haiku 5.5
output:
**Why I'm not dropping the busing project**

Some of you have already heard about this, and Jess, you've heard the most about it, so I'm writing it down once so I don't have to type it fifteen times.

Quick version for everyone else: I teach juniors in US History II. Every year they do an oral history project. They interview someone in their family or neighborhood about Boston in 1974–76, when busing and desegregation tore the city apart. They record a ten-minute interview and write a two-page reflection. I've done it for four years at Cobb Street, and nobody has ever complained.

This year a parent emailed the principal, Dr. Halvorsen, and copied a school committee member. Her main points were that the project "reopens wounds" and "pressures kids to judge their grandparents." I have a meeting with her and Dr. Halvorsen on Thursday the 19th at 3:15. The request, as I understand it, is that I quietly stop assigning it.

I'm not going to do that, and I want to explain why, because I don't think it's stubbornness and I don't think it's a grand stand.

I'll start by saying the parent has a point. Some of these kids are asking people they love to dig up things that hurt. A grandparent who was scared or ashamed or on the wrong side of something doesn't owe a teenager that story, and a kid who doesn't want to ask is not doing anything wrong by saying no. I'm not picking a fight with her. If I'd gotten that email from a family I'd have wanted a conversation too.

But here's what I keep coming back to. Two years ago a kid, D., interviewed his grandmother. She had driven a school bus in Southie in '74. She had never told anyone in her family about it. He played forty seconds of the recording for the class, and for about a full minute nobody said anything. It was the quietest room I've ever taught in, and it was not a bad quiet. Afterward a couple of kids told me their own families had never talked about any of it either. That's not something a textbook gives you. The textbook gives this whole fight one paragraph.

Last year a girl found out her uncle had thrown rocks at a bus when he was a teenager. She was really upset. We talked after class twice, once during her free period and once after school, and her reflection was the best thing I read all year. She wrote about being proud of her family and ashamed of them in the same breath, and about how she didn't know what to do with both. She got to figure that out with a reflection and a teacher. Without the assignment she would have just heard it at Thanksgiving, or never.

So yes, some kids will be uncomfortable. The kids who are most uncomfortable are often the ones who need this most, because the history is sitting in their own living rooms and they've been told, one way or another, not to touch it. But I don't get to force anybody into it. That's the line for me, and I'm not going to cross it. Nobody in my class gets forced to interview anyone.

Which is why the plan I'm bringing Thursday is to keep the project and add a real alternative. A kid can interview a librarian or archivist about the period, or use recorded interviews from past years if the people involved gave permission. Nobody has to call their grandmother if they don't want to. I think that's a fair version of the project, and it answers the pressure concern directly instead of just waving it off.

Now, Jess. I know you were trying to help. "It's one assignment, don't torch your job over it" is a very reasonable thing to say to someone you care about. We met in student teaching in 2012, and you've watched me get attached to things before. You left teaching in 2019 and you're not wrong that the building has leverage over me. I'm tenured, which helps, but Halvorsen still controls my schedule and who gets AP sections. I'm not pretending I'm not scared. I am. This isn't me being brave. It's me being scared and deciding I can live with the worse outcome more easily than the other one.

What I want you to understand is why it isn't just one assignment to me. It's the history of the city these kids live in. If I quietly drop it, I'm telling them that this is a thing you don't ask about. I don't want to teach them that, even if it's the safer thing for me.

I'm not asking you to agree with me. I'd just like you to know where I'm coming from, and that I'm not angry at you for saying what you said.

Thanks for reading, all of you. I'll text you Thursday after the meeting, Jess, whatever happens. I'll probably need to vent, and I'd like it to be you.

---

*A couple of notes for you before you post:* You might want to take out the students' initials and the detail about the uncle, or at least make them less identifiable, since this is going out while a complaint is still open. And the bit about Halvorsen controlling your schedule is accurate, but you may want to weigh whether it reads as a jab in writing.

reasons: The closing editorial note breaks the piece and speaks as an adviser rather than the teacher.
